title: Introductory Biochemistry
tagline: Meet the molecules of life, the rules they obey and the energy that keeps them running.
overview: The content follows the standard introductory biochemistry sequence at BSc level, arranged to prepare you for Level 3 Metabolism, Chemistry of Biomolecules and Gene Expression. We begin with water and buffers, move through amino acids, protein structure and folding, then enzyme catalysis and kinetics. Carbohydrates, lipids, membranes and nucleic acids come next, followed by bioenergetics and glycolysis, and finally the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. The aim is a sound conceptual map rather than exhaustive detail, with each unit signposting the Level 3 course where it is developed further.
whyItMatters: Every later course in your degree, from Metabolism I to Recombinant DNA Technology, assumes you can read a structure, rate a buffer, interpret an enzyme curve and follow the flow of energy through a pathway. This module builds that shared vocabulary and the habit of asking why a molecule has the shape it has and how that shape does a job.
careerLinks: Medicine and allied health sciences (via graduate entry)
studyTips: Draw the structures. You will never remember the 20 amino acids by reading them; group them by side-chain chemistry and draw them from memory in a table once a week.
Whenever you meet a number (pKa, Km, delta G), say out loud what it tells you and in which direction a change would push the system.
Redraw each pathway from a blank page, writing the enzyme class and cofactor on every arrow, then compare with the textbook.
Use the free structure viewers (PDB-101, RCSB 3D view) to rotate a real protein for each unit; shapes stick in memory better than text.
Link each topic to a disease: sickle cell, lactose intolerance, diabetes, mitochondrial disorders. A story makes the molecule memorable.

units.title: Water, pH and buffers
units.hook: Your blood stays within a fraction of a pH unit of 7.4 whether you are asleep, sprinting or fasting, and if it did not, your enzymes would stop working in minutes. The hero is the humble buffer, and the stage is water, the strangest and most important solvent in biology.
learningObjectives: Explain how the structure of water produces its solvent, thermal and cohesive properties.
Calculate pH, pOH and the ionisation state of a weak acid using Ka, pKa and the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.
Choose a suitable buffer for a given pH and explain how it resists change.
Describe how the bicarbonate system and proteins buffer blood and cells.

keyConcepts.definition: Each water molecule can donate two and accept two hydrogen bonds, creating a dynamic network that explains water's high boiling point, heat capacity and surface tension.
Describes a molecule with a polar (water-loving) end and a nonpolar (water-avoiding) end, such as a fatty acid or detergent; it is the basis of micelles and membranes.
The negative logarithm of hydrogen ion activity (concentration in dilute solutions); a one-unit change means a tenfold change in H+.
The pH at which an acid group is half protonated and half deprotonated; it measures acid strength independent of concentration.
pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]); it links pH, the pKa and the ratio of conjugate base to acid.
A mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base that resists pH change; it is most effective within about one pH unit of the pKa.
The amount of strong acid or base a buffer can absorb before the pH shifts substantially; it rises with concentration of the buffer components.

deeper.beginner: Water molecules are bent and slightly charged at each end, so they cling to each other and to anything else with charged or polar groups. Salts and sugars dissolve because water surrounds them; oils do not because they cannot bond with water. pH tells you how acidic a solution is. A buffer is a pair of molecules (a weak acid and its partner) that soaks up extra acid or base like a sponge so the pH stays steady.
deeper.intermediate: At pH equal to pKa the acid and base forms are equal, and at one unit away the ratio is 10 to 1, so a buffer works well roughly from pKa minus 1 to pKa plus 1. Phosphate (pKa2 about 7.2) is a good intracellular buffer; Tris (pKa about 8.1) and HEPES (about 7.5) are common in the laboratory. Blood is buffered mainly by bicarbonate, a system with an effective pKa of about 6.1 that is unusually powerful because CO2 can be exhaled and bicarbonate retained or excreted by the kidney. The side chain of histidine (pKa near 6) gives proteins such as haemoglobin significant buffering power.
deeper.advanced: The hydrophobic effect arises because nonpolar solutes disrupt water's hydrogen-bond network and force water into more ordered arrangements near small solutes, with enthalpy playing a larger role for large surfaces; it is not a direct attraction between nonpolar groups. Ball's review emphasises that water is an active participant in protein folding, enzyme catalysis and molecular recognition rather than an inert solvent. Also note that Henderson-Hasselbalch uses concentrations as a good approximation only for dilute solutions; in concentrated buffers activity coefficients and ionic strength shift the apparent pKa, and the pKa of a group inside a protein can differ by several units from its value in free solution.

commonMistakes: Thinking a buffer holds the pH exactly constant; it only resists change within its useful range and capacity.
Using a buffer whose pKa is more than one unit from the target pH.
Assuming pH 7 is the cell's only relevant pH; lysosomes (about pH 4.5 to 5), the stomach and the mitochondrial matrix differ widely.
Forgetting that pH is logarithmic: pH 5 is ten times more acidic than pH 6, not 'a bit' more.

selfCheck.question: A buffer is made with acetic acid (pKa 4.76) and acetate at equal concentrations. What is its pH?
selfCheck.explanation: When [A-] = [HA], the log term in Henderson-Hasselbalch is zero, so pH equals pKa, 4.76.

selfCheck.question: Which buffer would be best for an experiment at pH 7.2?
selfCheck.explanation: A buffer works best within one unit of its pKa, and phosphate's second pKa is almost exactly 7.2.

selfCheck.question: If the pH of a solution falls from 7.4 to 6.4, the hydrogen ion concentration has:
selfCheck.explanation: pH is a logarithmic scale, so a decrease of one unit corresponds to a tenfold increase in H+ concentration.

units.title: Amino acids and peptides
units.hook: Twenty small molecules, joined in different orders, make everything from the keratin of your hair to the haemoglobin carrying oxygen in your blood. Their personalities, charged, greasy, bendy or sulfur-containing, decide what each protein can do.
learningObjectives: Draw the general structure of an alpha-amino acid and its zwitterionic form at physiological pH.
Classify the 20 standard amino acids by side-chain properties.
Predict the net charge and isoelectric point of an amino acid or small peptide from pKa values.
Draw a peptide and name the N- and C-termini and the peptide bond.

keyConcepts.definition: A molecule with an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and a variable side chain (R) all attached to the central alpha carbon.
A molecule with both a positive and a negative charge but zero net charge, as amino acids are near neutral pH (NH3+ and COO-).
Nonpolar aliphatic (Gly, Ala, Val, Leu, Ile, Pro, Met), aromatic (Phe, Tyr, Trp), polar uncharged (Ser, Thr, Cys, Asn, Gln), positively charged (Lys, Arg, His) and negatively charged (Asp, Glu).
The pH at which a molecule has no net charge; for a simple amino acid it is the average of the two pKa values on either side of the neutral form.
An amide bond between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next, formed with loss of water.
All standard amino acids except glycine have a stereocentre at the alpha carbon, and those in proteins are the L-enantiomer.
A covalent S-S link formed by oxidation of two cysteine thiols, common in extracellular proteins.

deeper.beginner: Every amino acid has the same backbone: an amino group on one end, an acid group on the other, and a side chain that makes it different. At the pH of your cells the acid group has lost a proton and the amino group has gained one, so the molecule carries both charges. Joining amino acids end to end makes a chain called a peptide. Long chains are called polypeptides or proteins. The side chains stick out of the chain and decide how it folds.
deeper.intermediate: Typical pKa values are about 2 for the alpha-carboxyl, about 9 to 10 for the alpha-amino group, and side-chain values such as 3.9 (Asp), 4.1 (Glu), about 6 (His), 8.3 (Cys), 10.1 (Tyr), 10.5 (Lys) and 12.5 (Arg). Histidine is the only side chain with a pKa near physiological pH, which explains its role in enzyme catalysis and proton buffering. For acidic amino acids the pI is the average of the two lowest pKa values; for basic ones, the average of the two highest. Proline is special because its side chain loops back to the nitrogen, restricting backbone conformations; glycine is special because it lacks a side chain and is therefore the most flexible and the only achiral standard amino acid.
deeper.advanced: The peptide bond is nearly planar because of resonance, giving a rotational barrier that holds six atoms in a plane; only the phi and psi angles at each alpha carbon are free to vary, and steric constraints captured by the Ramachandran plot limit them to a small set of regions. Selenocysteine and pyrrolysine are incorporated through special recoding of stop codons and are sometimes called the 21st and 22nd amino acids, while many more residues, such as phosphoserine or hydroxyproline, arise from post-translational modification. Peptides can be sequenced by Edman degradation or, today, by tandem mass spectrometry.

commonMistakes: Drawing amino acids as uncharged at pH 7; the neutral form (NH2 and COOH together) is essentially absent in water.
Believing that histidine is always positively charged; at pH 7.4 it is mostly neutral.
Writing peptides starting at the C-terminus; by convention sequences are written N-terminus to C-terminus.
Confusing the pI with the pKa; the pI is where the net charge is zero, not a pKa value.

units.title: Protein structure and folding
units.hook: In 1949 Linus Pauling called sickle cell anaemia a 'molecular disease', and later work found it came from one amino acid change in haemoglobin, a glutamate swapped for a valine. One residue out of 146 changes how the molecule packs, and a whole red blood cell deforms. Shape is everything, and this unit is about how sequence becomes shape.
learningObjectives: Describe primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure with examples.
Explain alpha helices and beta sheets in terms of backbone hydrogen bonding.
List the forces that stabilise a folded protein and rank their roles.
Summarise Anfinsen's experiment and what it implies about sequence and structure.
Explain chaperones, misfolding and why structure prediction matters.

keyConcepts.definition: The sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide, determined by the gene.
A right-handed spiral stabilised by hydrogen bonds between the C=O of residue i and the N-H of residue i+4, with 3.6 residues per turn.
Strands lying side by side, held together by hydrogen bonds between strands, either parallel or antiparallel.
The overall three-dimensional fold of one polypeptide, stabilised by hydrophobic packing, hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions and sometimes disulfide bonds.
The arrangement of multiple polypeptide subunits, as in haemoglobin, a tetramer of two alpha and two beta chains.
A compact, independently folding region of a protein, often with a specific function.
A protein that helps others fold correctly or prevents aggregation, without being part of the final structure.
Loss of native structure by heat, extreme pH, detergents or chaotropes, usually with loss of function.

deeper.beginner: A protein is first just a string of amino acids. The string folds into local patterns, such as spirals (helices) and pleated sheets, and then these pieces fold into a compact three-dimensional shape. Water-fearing side chains tuck into the middle and water-loving ones sit on the outside. If the shape is lost, the protein cannot do its job. Some proteins have several chains that come together.
deeper.intermediate: The hydrophobic effect provides most of the driving force for folding, while hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and van der Waals contacts give specificity and the final fine-tuning; disulfide bridges stabilise secreted proteins. Anfinsen showed that ribonuclease A, after being denatured and reduced, spontaneously refolded and regained activity when the denaturant was removed, which led to the thermodynamic hypothesis that the native state is the minimum free energy state determined by the sequence. Levinthal's paradox points out that proteins cannot fold by random search, so folding pathways must be funnelled. In cells, chaperones such as Hsp70 and chaperonins assist folding of newly made proteins, and misfolded proteins are tagged for degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
deeper.advanced: The helix and sheet were predicted by Pauling, Corey and Branson from the planarity of the peptide bond and hydrogen-bonding geometry before any protein structure was solved. Folding is better described as a funnel-shaped energy landscape than a single pathway, and some proteins are intrinsically disordered yet functional. Misfolding underlies diseases such as amyloidosis and prion disorders, where beta-rich aggregates are very stable. Deep-learning methods such as AlphaFold now predict structures of single chains with accuracy comparable to experiment for many proteins, but they do not directly explain folding pathways, dynamics, or the effect of every mutation.

commonMistakes: Thinking that all proteins fold alone and spontaneously; many need chaperones in the crowded cell.
Calling beta sheets 'weaker' than helices; stability depends on context, not on type of secondary structure.
Treating denaturation as the breaking of peptide bonds; it disrupts non-covalent folding, not the backbone.
Assuming that every disulfide bond forms in the cytosol; the reducing cytosol disfavours them, and they form mainly in oxidising compartments such as the ER or outside the cell.

selfCheck.explanation: Hydrogen bonds in an alpha helix link the C=O of residue i to the N-H of residue i+4, equivalently the N-H of residue i to the C=O of residue i-4.

Peptide bonds are broken by urea
selfCheck.explanation: After denaturation and reduction, ribonuclease refolded and regained activity once the denaturant was removed, so sequence alone specified its structure under those conditions.

options: A charged residue replaced by a nonpolar residue on the surface
A hydrophobic residue replaced by a charged one
A change in quaternary structure only
selfCheck.explanation: Glu is negatively charged while Val is hydrophobic. The new surface hydrophobic patch lets deoxy-haemoglobin molecules stick together and polymerise.

units.title: Enzymes: catalysis, kinetics and inhibition
units.hook: Without an enzyme, a peptide bond in water would last for hundreds of years; with a protease, it is cut in a fraction of a second. Enzymes are the reason chemistry that would take geological time can finish inside a living cell between two heartbeats.
learningObjectives: Explain how enzymes lower activation energy without changing equilibrium.
Describe lock-and-key, induced fit and transition-state stabilisation models.
Interpret a Michaelis-Menten plot and a Lineweaver-Burk plot to obtain Vmax and Km.
Distinguish competitive, uncompetitive and noncompetitive inhibition from kinetic data.
Describe general catalytic strategies and the roles of cofactors.

keyConcepts.definition: The energy barrier between substrate and product; enzymes lower it by stabilising the transition state.
The region of the enzyme where substrate binds and catalysis occurs, made of residues that may be far apart in the sequence but close in the folded protein.
v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]); it describes initial rate versus substrate concentration for simple enzymes.
The substrate concentration at which the rate is half of Vmax; roughly a measure of affinity (lower Km often means tighter binding) under simple assumptions.
kcat = Vmax/[E]total, the number of substrate molecules converted per active site per second; kcat/Km measures catalytic efficiency.
The inhibitor competes with substrate for the active site; apparent Km rises while Vmax is unchanged.
The inhibitor binds elsewhere and lowers the effective amount of active enzyme; Vmax falls while Km is unchanged (in the pure case).
Non-protein helpers: metal ions (cofactors) or organic molecules such as NAD+ and coenzyme A (coenzymes), often derived from vitamins.

deeper.beginner: An enzyme is a protein that speeds up one reaction by holding the reacting molecules in just the right way. It does not change what the reaction gives, only how fast it gets there. If you give an enzyme more substrate, the rate goes up and then levels off because all the enzyme molecules are busy. The Km tells you roughly how much substrate you need to get halfway to that top speed.
deeper.intermediate: Michaelis-Menten kinetics assume that E and S form an ES complex in rapid equilibrium or at steady state, and that the measured rate is the initial rate when product is negligible. In a double-reciprocal (Lineweaver-Burk) plot, 1/v against 1/[S] gives a straight line with intercept 1/Vmax and slope Km/Vmax. Competitive inhibitors change the slope but not the y-intercept; noncompetitive inhibitors change the y-intercept but not the x-intercept; uncompetitive inhibitors change both, giving parallel lines. Catalytic strategies include proximity and orientation effects, general acid-base catalysis, covalent catalysis (as with the Ser-His-Asp triad of chymotrypsin), metal-ion catalysis and, above all, preferential binding of the transition state, which Knowles argued is what makes enzymes 'not different, just better' than other catalysts.
deeper.advanced: Fischer's lock-and-key analogy emphasised complementarity; Koshland's induced fit recognised that the enzyme changes shape upon binding, and modern views invoke conformational ensembles and dynamics. kcat/Km values approach the diffusion limit of about 10^8 to 10^9 per molar per second for 'perfect' enzymes such as triose phosphate isomerase, which means evolution has optimised them until the encounter rate is rate-limiting. Lineweaver-Burk plots are useful for diagnosis but statistically poor for parameter estimation, because they distort errors at low substrate concentration; non-linear regression on the original equation is preferred. Michaelis and Menten's 1913 paper also introduced the careful control of pH and mutarotation that made quantitative enzyme kinetics possible.

commonMistakes: Saying an enzyme 'makes a reaction happen'; it accelerates a thermodynamically favourable reaction but cannot make an unfavourable one go.
Reading Km as a pure affinity constant; it is equal to the dissociation constant only under specific assumptions.
Calling the Lineweaver-Burk plot the best way to fit data; use it for visual diagnosis only.
Confusing competitive inhibition (Km changes) with noncompetitive (Vmax changes).

selfCheck.question: A competitive inhibitor is added to an enzyme reaction. Compared with no inhibitor, what happens to the apparent Km and Vmax?
selfCheck.explanation: Because high substrate concentrations can outcompete the inhibitor, Vmax is reached eventually, but more substrate is needed to reach half Vmax, so the apparent Km goes up.

selfCheck.question: What does an enzyme change about a reaction?
options: The free energy difference between substrate and product
selfCheck.explanation: Catalysts lower the activation energy barrier, increasing rate in both directions, but leave equilibrium and overall free energy change unchanged.

selfCheck.question: At [S] equal to Km, the rate of a Michaelis-Menten enzyme is:
selfCheck.explanation: Substituting [S] = Km into v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) gives v = Vmax/2.

units.title: Carbohydrates, lipids and biological membranes
units.hook: A cell is a bag of chemistry only because a film two molecules thick keeps the inside in and the outside out. The same fats that you might want to avoid in your diet build that film, and the sugars that fuel your brain are also the code on the surface of every cell.
learningObjectives: Draw the open-chain and ring forms of glucose and explain alpha and beta anomers.
Distinguish glycogen, starch and cellulose by glycosidic linkage and function.
Describe the structures of fatty acids, triacylglycerols, phospholipids and cholesterol.
Explain how the lipid bilayer forms and how the fluid mosaic model describes membranes.
Describe how temperature, cholesterol and unsaturation influence membrane fluidity.

keyConcepts.definition: A simple sugar, such as glucose, fructose or galactose; named by number of carbons and whether the carbonyl is an aldehyde (aldose) or ketone (ketose).
An acetal linkage between the anomeric carbon of a sugar and an oxygen of another molecule, formed with loss of water.
Starch and glycogen (alpha-1,4 chains with alpha-1,6 branches) store glucose; cellulose (beta-1,4) gives rigid structure because its chains lie straight and hydrogen-bond into fibres.
A long hydrocarbon chain with a terminal carboxylic acid; saturated chains pack tightly, while cis double bonds put kinks in the chain.
Glycerol esterified to three fatty acids; the main fuel store, with more energy per gram than carbohydrate because it is more reduced and stored without water.
Glycerol or sphingosine backbone with two hydrophobic tails and a polar phosphate-containing head group, the basic building block of membranes.
Membranes are two-dimensional fluids in which lipids and proteins can diffuse laterally; proteins are embedded or attached, forming a dynamic mosaic.
A rigid sterol that inserts between phospholipids, modulating fluidity: it reduces motion at high temperature and disrupts tight packing at low temperature.

deeper.beginner: Sugars are rings of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Many glucose molecules joined together make starch or glycogen for energy storage, or cellulose for the strong fibres of plants. Fats and oils are made from long chains of carbon and hydrogen attached to glycerol. A phospholipid has a water-loving head and two water-fearing tails; in water, these molecules arrange into a double layer with the heads facing out and tails hidden inside. That double layer is the basic membrane of every cell.
deeper.intermediate: The cyclic hemiacetal form of glucose has an anomeric carbon at C1; in the alpha anomer the OH is axial (trans to the CH2OH group on the ring), and in the beta anomer it is equatorial. Starch contains amylose (unbranched alpha-1,4) and amylopectin (branched with alpha-1,6 at about every 24 to 30 residues); glycogen is more highly branched and so is mobilised faster at many ends. Membranes are asymmetric: different phospholipids are enriched in the inner and outer leaflets, and glycolipids and glycoproteins face outward. Membrane proteins are integral (crossing the bilayer, often as alpha helices of about 20 hydrophobic residues) or peripheral. Lactose, sucrose and maltose differ by their glycosidic linkages: lactose is galactose beta-1,4 glucose, sucrose is glucose alpha-1 to fructose beta-2, and maltose is glucose alpha-1,4 glucose.
deeper.advanced: Singer and Nicolson's 1972 model explained how proteins and lipids could mix, but modern work shows that membranes are crowded and heterogeneous, with lipid-protein domains, cytoskeletal corrals and transient nanoscale assemblies that can influence signalling; the term 'lipid raft' remains debated. Membrane curvature, lipid composition and transport are linked, and lipid asymmetry is actively maintained by flippases, floppases and scramblases; exposure of phosphatidylserine on the outer leaflet is an 'eat me' signal for apoptotic cells. Cellulose's beta linkage requires cellulase enzymes that animals lack, so ruminant animals and termites depend on gut microbes for digestion.

commonMistakes: Drawing glucose only in the open-chain form; in solution more than 99 percent is cyclic.
Mixing up alpha and beta anomers, or alpha and beta glycosidic linkages; the same descriptors apply to the OH at C1.
Saying membranes are static; lipids diffuse laterally very quickly, although flipping between leaflets without enzymes is very slow.
Believing that unsaturated fats are always bad; cis-unsaturated lipids maintain membrane fluidity and are essential.

selfCheck.question: Which polysaccharide has beta-1,4 glycosidic linkages and cannot be digested by humans?
selfCheck.explanation: Cellulose consists of glucose joined by beta-1,4 linkages; human digestive enzymes cannot cleave them.

selfCheck.question: What effect does a cis double bond in a membrane fatty acid have?
options: Increases packing density and melting point
Introduces a kink that increases membrane fluidity
Prevents the phospholipid from forming a bilayer
selfCheck.explanation: The bend produced by a cis double bond prevents tight packing of tails, lowering the melting point and increasing fluidity.

selfCheck.question: Why do phospholipids form bilayers spontaneously in water?
options: Hydrophobic tails are shielded from water while polar heads interact with it
selfCheck.explanation: The amphipathic structure leads to a lowest free energy arrangement in which hydrophobic tails are buried and polar heads face water; no energy input or enzyme is needed.

units.title: Nucleotides and nucleic acids
units.hook: In 1953 a short note of about a thousand words in Nature described the structure of DNA and ended with one of the most famous understatements in science: that the pairing they proposed immediately suggested a copying mechanism. Every cell division since has used that mechanism, and the chemistry behind it is simple enough to draw from memory.
learningObjectives: Draw the structure of a nucleotide and identify its sugar, base and phosphate.
Explain how nucleotides join into a polynucleotide strand with 5' to 3' polarity.
Describe base pairing, antiparallel strands and the major and minor grooves of the double helix.
Compare DNA and RNA in structure, stability and role.
Explain how GC content and salt affect the melting temperature of DNA.

keyConcepts.definition: A nitrogenous base joined to a five-carbon sugar and one or more phosphate groups; a nucleoside lacks the phosphate.
Adenine and guanine are purines (double ring); cytosine, thymine and uracil are pyrimidines (single ring).
A link between the 3' hydroxyl of one nucleotide and the 5' phosphate of the next, forming the sugar-phosphate backbone.
A pairs with T (two hydrogen bonds) or U in RNA, and G pairs with C (three hydrogen bonds), which allows each strand to specify the other.
The two strands of a double helix run in opposite 5' to 3' directions.
Spaces between the sugar-phosphate backbones where edges of the bases are exposed; proteins read DNA sequence mainly through the major groove.
The temperature at which half of a DNA duplex has separated; it rises with GC content and with ionic strength.
Usually single-stranded, contains ribose with a 2' OH and uracil instead of thymine; the 2' OH makes RNA more susceptible to hydrolysis.

deeper.beginner: DNA is a long chain made of four building blocks, A, T, G and C. Each block has a base, a sugar and a phosphate. The phosphate and sugar form a backbone and the bases stick out. Two chains pair up so that A always sits opposite T and G opposite C, and the pair twists into a double helix. RNA is similar but has a different sugar, uses U instead of T, and is usually single stranded.
deeper.intermediate: In B-DNA, the most common form in cells, the helix is right-handed with a diameter of about 2 nm, a rise of 0.34 nm per base pair and about 10 to 10.5 base pairs per turn. Base stacking contributes as much to stability as base-pair hydrogen bonding, and the hydrophobic effect pushes the bases into the centre. Chargaff's rules (A = T and G = C in double-stranded DNA) reflect pairing. DNA is stable partly because of the missing 2' OH and because of the negatively charged backbone, which repels hydroxide; RNA is more reactive, which suits its transient roles. Many RNAs fold into complex three-dimensional shapes, including catalytic RNAs (ribozymes) and the ribosome's rRNA.
deeper.advanced: Watson and Crick built their model using Rosalind Franklin's and Maurice Wilkins's X-ray diffraction data together with Chargaff's base ratios and the tautomeric forms of bases; their note stressed that specific pairing suggests a copying mechanism. Alternative forms exist: A-DNA is favoured in dehydrating conditions and in DNA-RNA hybrids, and left-handed Z-DNA appears in alternating purine-pyrimidine sequences under high salt or negative supercoiling. Spontaneous chemical damage, such as deamination of cytosine to uracil and loss of purines (depurination), occurs at measurable rates, which is why repair systems are essential.

commonMistakes: Writing sequences without noting the 5' and 3' ends; the two strands of a duplex are antiparallel.
Saying that A-T pairs are 'weaker' because they have fewer hydrogen bonds without remembering that stacking interactions matter as well.
Mixing up nucleoside and nucleotide, or purine and pyrimidine; remember that pyrimidines contain Y (cytosine, thymine, uracil).
Assuming RNA is always single-stranded; it often forms local double-stranded regions in hairpins.

selfCheck.question: How many hydrogen bonds join a G-C base pair?
selfCheck.explanation: G-C pairs form three hydrogen bonds, while A-T pairs form two, which is one reason GC-rich DNA has a higher melting temperature.

selfCheck.question: Which feature chemically distinguishes RNA from DNA?
options: RNA has a 2' hydroxyl on the sugar and uracil rather than thymine
selfCheck.explanation: RNA contains ribose (with a 2' OH) and uracil, whereas DNA has deoxyribose and thymine.

selfCheck.question: The phosphodiester bond in a nucleic acid joins:
options: The 5' phosphate of one nucleotide to the 3' OH of the next
The 2' and 5' carbons of the same sugar
selfCheck.explanation: The backbone links the 3' hydroxyl of one nucleotide to the 5' phosphate of the next, giving each strand a 5' to 3' direction.

units.title: Bioenergetics, ATP and glycolysis
units.hook: Your body hydrolyses and remakes roughly its own weight in ATP every day, yet only tens of grams of ATP exist at any one moment. That frantic recycling is the currency exchange of life, and glycolysis, a ten-step pathway shared by almost every organism, is where it first pays out.
learningObjectives: Use delta G, delta G0' and the reaction quotient to decide the direction of a reaction.
Explain how coupling to ATP hydrolysis drives otherwise unfavourable reactions.
Describe the overall logic of catabolism and anabolism and the role of NAD+/NADH.
Outline the investment and payoff phases of glycolysis and its net yield.
Identify the key regulated steps and explain how fermentation regenerates NAD+.

keyConcepts.definition: The energy available to do work; a reaction is spontaneous in the forward direction when delta G is negative.
Free energy change under standard conditions at pH 7; the actual delta G depends on concentrations via delta G = delta G0' + RT ln Q.
Linking an unfavourable reaction to a favourable one (often ATP hydrolysis) so that the sum has a negative delta G.
The cell's energy carrier; hydrolysis of its terminal phosphate releases about 30.5 kJ/mol under standard conditions and more in cells because ATP is kept far above equilibrium.
A coenzyme pair that carries electrons (as hydride) from oxidation reactions to the respiratory chain or to biosynthesis.
Direct transfer of a phosphate group from a high-energy substrate to ADP, as in glycolysis.
The main regulatory enzyme of glycolysis; inhibited by ATP and citrate, activated by AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate.
Pathways such as pyruvate to lactate or ethanol that regenerate NAD+ so glycolysis can continue without oxygen.

deeper.beginner: Cells need energy to build things and move things, and they get it by breaking down food. The energy is passed around in a small molecule called ATP, like a rechargeable battery. Glycolysis breaks one glucose (six carbons) into two pyruvate (three carbons each). Along the way it spends two ATP and makes four, so the net gain is two, plus two NADH, which are carriers of high-energy electrons.
deeper.intermediate: Free energy of a reaction under cell conditions depends on concentrations, so a reaction with a small positive delta G0' can still go forward when product is removed quickly. ATP hydrolysis is used by enzymes to drive reactions by transferring phosphate to a substrate (making it more reactive) rather than by 'releasing energy into space'. Glycolysis has an investment phase (hexokinase and phosphofructokinase use ATP, and aldolase splits fructose 1,6-bisphosphate into two triose phosphates) and a payoff phase (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase makes NADH; phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase make ATP). The three steps with large negative delta G in cells (hexokinase, PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase) are the regulated ones, and they are bypassed in gluconeogenesis.
deeper.advanced: Free energy of ATP hydrolysis in cells is typically cited as about -50 to -65 kJ/mol because the ATP/ADP ratio and phosphate levels are held far from equilibrium; Mg2+ binding to the polyphosphate also changes the value. 'High-energy bond' is a misleading phrase: the energy comes from the difference between reactants and products in solution. Glycolysis flux is controlled by many enzymes, not just one, as described by metabolic control analysis, and it integrates with insulin and glucagon signalling, hypoxia-inducible factor and the Warburg effect in cancer cells, where glycolysis is high even in oxygen.

commonMistakes: Using delta G0' to decide the direction of a reaction in the cell; actual delta G depends on concentrations.
Saying glycolysis produces four ATP net; the net yield is two ATP per glucose (four made, two spent).
Thinking that ATP hydrolysis alone 'releases energy' without a coupling mechanism; the energy must be transduced by an enzyme.
Forgetting that NAD+ must be regenerated; without it glycolysis stops.

selfCheck.question: What is the net ATP yield of glycolysis per molecule of glucose (by substrate-level phosphorylation)?
selfCheck.explanation: Two ATP are used in the investment phase and four are formed in the payoff phase, so the net is two ATP per glucose.

selfCheck.question: Why do cells need lactate fermentation in the absence of oxygen?
options: To produce more ATP in the mitochondrion
To regenerate NAD+ so glycolysis can continue
selfCheck.explanation: Reducing pyruvate to lactate oxidises NADH back to NAD+, which glycolysis requires at the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase step.

selfCheck.question: A reaction has delta G0' = +10 kJ/mol. Under what condition can it proceed forward in cells?
options: If its product is rapidly consumed so that the actual delta G is negative
selfCheck.explanation: Actual delta G includes the RT ln Q term; keeping products low (or coupling to ATP hydrolysis) can make the actual delta G negative.

units.title: The citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation
units.hook: Inside every mitochondrion a tiny rotary motor spins at around a hundred times a second, driven by protons flowing down a gradient, and it makes most of your ATP. The idea that a proton gradient, not a chemical intermediate, links respiration to ATP synthesis was so strange that Peter Mitchell was ignored for years before he won the Nobel Prize.
learningObjectives: Describe how pyruvate is converted into acetyl-CoA and enters the citric acid cycle.
State the inputs and outputs of one turn of the cycle and where reduced coenzymes are made.
Describe the electron transport chain complexes and how they create a proton gradient.
Explain chemiosmotic coupling and how ATP synthase works.
Estimate the ATP yield from glucose and discuss uncouplers and inhibitors.

keyConcepts.definition: A multi-enzyme complex that converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, releasing CO2 and producing NADH; it links glycolysis to the cycle.
A cycle in which acetyl-CoA is joined to oxaloacetate to give citrate; each turn releases two CO2 and yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP or ATP.
Protein complexes I to IV in the inner mitochondrial membrane that pass electrons from NADH and FADH2 to oxygen, pumping protons as they do.
The combined chemical (pH) and electrical gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane that stores energy for ATP synthesis.
A rotary enzyme (F0F1) in which proton flow through F0 turns a central stalk and drives ATP formation in F1.
Mitchell's proposal that electron transport pumps protons to build a gradient that is then used to make ATP.
A molecule (such as 2,4-dinitrophenol or the protein UCP1) that dissipates the proton gradient so energy is released as heat rather than ATP.
The number of ATP made per oxygen atom reduced; current estimates are about 2.5 for NADH and 1.5 for FADH2.

deeper.beginner: After glycolysis the carbon from sugar is turned into acetyl-CoA and burned in a cycle that releases CO2 and loads up electron carriers (NADH and FADH2). Those carriers drop their electrons into a chain of proteins in the inner mitochondrial membrane. As electrons move down the chain to oxygen, protons are pumped across the membrane. The protons then rush back through ATP synthase, which spins like a turbine and makes ATP.
deeper.intermediate: One turn of the cycle starts with citrate synthase joining acetyl-CoA to oxaloacetate; subsequent steps release CO2 at isocitrate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and produce succinate, fumarate, malate and finally oxaloacetate again. Complex I and II feed electrons to ubiquinone; complex III passes them via cytochrome c to complex IV, which reduces oxygen to water. Complexes I, III and IV pump protons; complex II does not. Roughly 10 protons are pumped per NADH and about 4 protons are needed per ATP (including transport), giving the P/O ratios above and about 30 to 32 ATP per glucose in current estimates, rather than the older figure of 36 to 38. Cyanide and carbon monoxide inhibit complex IV; rotenone inhibits complex I; oligomycin blocks ATP synthase.
deeper.advanced: Mitchell's 1961 proposal predicted that an intact membrane and a gradient were essential, and experiments with artificial gradients (Jagendorf's acid-bath experiment in chloroplasts) and with reconstituted vesicles confirmed it. Structures of respiratory supercomplexes and the ATP synthase rotary mechanism (Boyer's binding-change model, Walker's structure) have since filled in the details. Control of oxidative phosphorylation by ADP availability (respiratory control) means that ATP use sets the pace of the whole process, and reactive oxygen species leak from complexes I and III, linking mitochondria to ageing, signalling and disease.

commonMistakes: Claiming that the citric acid cycle directly requires oxygen; it needs NAD+ and FAD, which are regenerated by the respiratory chain, so it stops without oxygen indirectly.
Saying that the ATP yield per glucose is 36 or 38 as a fixed figure; modern estimates are about 30 to 32.
Believing that electrons flowing through the chain make ATP directly; they build a proton gradient, and the gradient makes the ATP.
Forgetting that protons are pumped into the intermembrane space, not into the matrix.

selfCheck.question: How many NADH are produced per turn of the citric acid cycle?
selfCheck.explanation: Each turn yields 3 NADH (at isocitrate, alpha-ketoglutarate and malate dehydrogenases), 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP or ATP.

selfCheck.question: What directly drives ATP synthesis by ATP synthase?
options: Flow of protons down their gradient through F0
Direct transfer of phosphate from NADH
selfCheck.explanation: Protons flowing back into the matrix through F0 rotate the central stalk, which causes conformational changes in F1 that make ATP.

selfCheck.question: Which respiratory chain complex does NOT pump protons?
selfCheck.explanation: Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) passes electrons from FADH2 to ubiquinone without pumping protons.
